prs.title: Fix `token_expiry_time` upon context initialization for stored tokens.
prs.author: keurcien
prs.reason: [llm] cluster primary: After tokens are loaded from storage on init, `token_expiry_time` is never repopulated (only the raw `OAuthToken` is restored), so `is_token_valid()`/`is_token_expired()` misjudge a stale token as valid. This causes the proactive refresh path to be skipped and forces the client into a full interactive re-authorization instead of a silent refresh whenever the process restarts and the access token has actually expired. (2 PRs)

This causes the proactive refresh path to be skipped and forces the client into a full interactive re-authorization instead of a silent refresh whenever the process restarts and the access token has actually expired. (2 PRs)
prs.cluster_pick_reason: #1784 fixes the root cause directly in `_initialize()` with a 4-line change that calls the existing `update_token_expiry()` helper as soon as stored tokens are loaded, and ships a regression test fixture (`expired_tokens`) exercising the expired-on-load case. #2875's own inline comment explicitly names this same gap ('a provider reloaded from storage never restores token_expiry_time') as its motivation, but instead of restoring the state it adds a ~15-line workaround in `async_auth_flow` that tries a stored refresh token on 401 before falling back to full re-auth — a larger, symptom-level patch to a hot code path. Once #1784 lands, the earlier proactive-refresh branch in `async_auth_flow` correctly fires on expiry, making #2875's added 401 fallback branch redundant for the scenario it was written to address.

prs.cluster_pick_reason: #2492 solves this by persisting `oauth_metadata` through two new optional `TokenStorage` methods (`get_oauth_metadata`/`set_oauth_metadata`) with no-op/None defaults, so it's backward compatible with existing storage implementations and eliminates the rediscovery round-trip entirely on subsequent restarts. #3263 instead re-runs AS metadata discovery inside the refresh path on every cold start (guarded only by an in-memory `eager_discovery_attempted` flag that itself resets on each restart, so the network round-trip recurs every restart), and bundles in a separate issuer-binding validation concern on top of the same code path, making it a larger and riskier change to the shared refresh control flow for the same underlying gap. prs.title: Fix substring matches in WWW-Authenticate parsing
prs.author: Whning0513
prs.reason: [llm] cluster primary: The existing WWW-Authenticate parser in src/mcp/client/auth/utils.py used a naive/regex approach that matched auth-param values as substrings instead of parsing proper comma-separated, quote-aware tokens — e.g. it could mis-parse a header containing multiple challenges/schemes or quoted commas within a parameter value. Both PRs replace this with a hand-rolled, quote- and escape-aware comma splitter over the header value. (2 PRs)

prs.cluster_pick_reason: Both PRs add near-identical quote/escape-aware comma-splitting tokenizers for the WWW-Authenticate header (compare _iter_www_auth_params in #3012 vs _split_www_authenticate_segments in #3041 — same character-by-character quote/escape state machine). #3041 goes a step further with _extract_bearer_auth_params, which isolates the Bearer challenge's params by scheme before collecting them, so it correctly handles headers containing multiple challenges/schemes (e.g. 'Bearer ..., DPoP ...') in one header value. #3012's _iter_www_auth_params only splits everything after the first space, so it would misparse a header value if a second scheme's challenge follows the first — the exact substring/boundary bug both PRs are titled around fixing.

members.title: fix(stdio): allow configurable memory stream buffer size
members.author: yaowubarbara
members.reason: [llm] duplicates #2654: Both touch the write_stream (and read_stream) memory-object-stream buffer size in stdio_server, which defaults to 0 (unbuffered/rendezvous). #2654 diagnoses this as the root cause of a real deadlock/blocking bug: a handler can't queue its final JSON-RPC response while stdout_writer is still flushing an earlier progress notification, because the channel has zero capacity. It fixes this concretely by hardcoding the write-stream buffer to 1, with a new regression test (BlockingStdout) that reproduces the stall. #2215 addresses the same parameter (buffer size 0) but only exposes it as a caller-supplied argument (read_stream_buffer_size/write_stream_buffer_size) while leaving the default at 0 - so it doesn't actually fix the progress-notification bug unless a caller opts in explicitly. Both diffs modify the same construction line for write_stream (and read_stream), so merging both as-is would conflict.

clusters.pick_reason: 2395's diff is a small, self-contained 14-line change to the existing bail-out branch that directly resolves the specific hung JSON-RPC request by id, leaving other in-flight requests on the same connection unaffected. 3098's fix instead unwinds a StreamableHTTPError out of an ExceptionGroup and would raise/propagate through the task group, which is a broader-blast-radius change (affects the whole transport context, not just the one disconnected request); it also touches an unrelated line (reverting `from __future__ import annotations as _annotations` back to the unaliased form), which is more likely to hit merge conflicts against unrelated import changes and suggests the branch is based on a different point in history.

members.title: Fix infinite reconnection loop in StreamableHTTP client
members.author: Dharit13
members.reason: [llm] cluster primary: SSE reconnection failure in _handle_reconnection is not surfaced properly to the caller: when reconnection is abandoned, the pending JSON-RPC request just hangs. #2395 fixes this in the existing 'max attempts exceeded' bail-out branch by sending a correlated JSONRPCError (INTERNAL_ERROR) keyed to the disconnected request's id via ctx.read_stream_writer, unblocking only that request while leaving the rest of the connection intact. #3098 addresses the same reconnection-failure symptom from the exception-propagation side, adding a recursive _unwrap_exception() helper to pull a StreamableHTTPError out of anyio's ExceptionGroup wrapping so a clean exception type is raised instead. clusters.pick_reason: #2492 solves this by persisting `oauth_metadata` through two new optional `TokenStorage` methods (`get_oauth_metadata`/`set_oauth_metadata`) with no-op/None defaults, so it's backward compatible with existing storage implementations and eliminates the rediscovery round-trip entirely on subsequent restarts. #3263 instead re-runs AS metadata discovery inside the refresh path on every cold start (guarded only by an in-memory `eager_discovery_attempted` flag that itself resets on each restart, so the network round-trip recurs every restart), and bundles in a separate issuer-binding validation concern on top of the same code path, making it a larger and riskier change to the shared refresh control flow for the same underlying gap. The issuer-binding check in #3263 is a distinct security hardening that could be proposed independently of the restart/refresh fix.

members.author: Bartok9
members.reason: [llm] cluster primary: Both PRs patch the exact same `if has_previous_tool_use and previous_content:` block in validate_tool_use_result_messages, both triggered by the same underlying report (#2960): a tool_use not followed by any tool_result currently raises "ids of tool_result blocks and tool_use blocks from previous message do not match" because tool_result_ids ends up empty. However the two PRs resolve it in opposite, mutually-exclusive ways: #2962 adds a `has_tool_results` guard so the id-matching check is skipped entirely when there are no tool_results, meaning no error is raised at all (citing SEP-1577: tool_result must follow tool_use, but tool_use need not be followed by tool_result). #3053 instead adds an explicit `if not has_tool_results: raise ValueError(...)` branch that still raises in that same case, just with a clearer message. Their own new tests assert opposite outcomes for the identical scenario (one asserts 'Should not raise', the other asserts a raise), so both cannot be merged. (2 PRs)

clusters.pick_reason: Both PRs add near-identical quote/escape-aware comma-splitting tokenizers for the WWW-Authenticate header (compare _iter_www_auth_params in #3012 vs _split_www_authenticate_segments in #3041 — same character-by-character quote/escape state machine). #3041 goes a step further with _extract_bearer_auth_params, which isolates the Bearer challenge's params by scheme before collecting them, so it correctly handles headers containing multiple challenges/schemes (e.g. 'Bearer ..., DPoP ...') in one header value. #3012's _iter_www_auth_params only splits everything after the first space, so it would misparse a header value if a second scheme's challenge follows the first — the exact substring/boundary bug both PRs are titled around fixing.

members.author: tarunag10

clusters.pick_reason: #2654 changes the default write-stream buffer from 0 to 1, which actually resolves the blocking bug without requiring caller configuration, and ships a targeted regression test (BlockingStdout) proving the deadlock scenario. #2215 only threads through a configurable parameter with the default left at 0, so it doesn't fix the underlying blocking behavior unless every caller remembers to opt in - it's a superset API surface but a no-op fix by default, and its diff is against an older version of stdio.py (predates the create_context_streams refactor visible in #2552/#2654), so it would need to be rebased regardless.

members.title: fix(stdio): allow configurable memory stream buffer size
members.author: yaowubarbara
members.reason: [llm] duplicates #2654: Both touch the write_stream (and read_stream) memory-object-stream buffer size in stdio_server, which defaults to 0 (unbuffered/rendezvous). #2654 diagnoses this as the root cause of a real deadlock/blocking bug: a handler can't queue its final JSON-RPC response while stdout_writer is still flushing an earlier progress notification, because the channel has zero capacity. It fixes this concretely by hardcoding the write-stream buffer to 1, with a new regression test (BlockingStdout) that reproduces the stall. #2215 addresses the same parameter (buffer size 0) but only exposes it as a caller-supplied argument (read_stream_buffer_size/write_stream_buffer_size) while leaving the default at 0 - so it doesn't actually fix the progress-notification bug unless a caller opts in explicitly. Both diffs modify the same construction line for write_stream (and read_stream), so merging both as-is would conflict.
